books.section: Topic 1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: The French had no goods that Native peoples wanted to trade for.
options.misconception: Iron tools and cloth were in high demand; trade is the reason the French came.

options.text: Native nations had already conquered the French settlements on the coast.
options.misconception: No such conquest happened; the French stayed small and traded.

options.text: The French king ordered all traders to avoid any contact with Native peoples.
options.misconception: The opposite is true: French traders lived and worked alongside Native peoples.

options.text: Furs required Native hunters and trappers, so cooperation paid better than conquest.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what the French wanted. Furs, which came from Native hunting and trapping.
2. Ask who could supply them. Only Native hunters knew the land and the animals.
3. Ask what conquest would do. It would destroy the very people the trade needed.
4. Rule out the rest. No royal ban, no Native conquest, and no shortage of desirable goods explain the pattern.
Remember: when a business needs its partners alive and working, partnership is the strategy.
rationales.D: The fur trade ran on Native skill: hunting and trapping were Native work. Conquest would have killed the workforce, so traders partnered with the people they needed.
rationales.A: Iron tools and cloth were exactly what Native peoples wanted. French goods drove the trade from the start.
rationales.B: Native nations did not conquer French settlements. The French presence was small and commercial, not a conquered colony.
rationales.C: The French king never ordered traders to avoid Native peoples. Partnership, not avoidance, was the French pattern.

stem: Why did French traders build partnerships with Native nations instead of conquering them?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing 5 Steps to a 5 2024 Chapter 6 (Cartier on the St. Lawrence) and Princeton Review Chapter 6 (French fur trade and Native alliances).
stimulus.text: From the early 1500s, French fishermen and traders along the North Atlantic coast exchanged iron tools and cloth for furs with Native peoples. Jacques Cartier explored the St. Lawrence River in the 1530s and found Native peoples already trading furs. The fur trade depended on Native hunters and trappers, so French traders built partnerships with Native nations instead of large settler colonies, mines, or missions.
